claims: T1 definition: a fully developed fictional character created by an author to write under a distinct identity, with biography, physical appearance, philosophy and writing style
T2 pseudonyms (pen names): simply a false name used by an author who continues to write as themselves
T3 heteronyms: independent personae operating outside the author's own personality, sometimes critiquing or translating each other's work
T4 the creator writing as themselves is the 'orthonym'

T5 Pessoa coined the term and invented dozens of heteronyms: Caeiro (pastoral, anti-philosophical, the 'master'), Reis (neoclassical, formal, pagan worldview), Campos (exuberant modernist engineer and futurist poet)
T6 Kierkegaard used numerous pseudonymous/heteronymous authors (Johannes de Silentio, Anti-Climacus) to present conflicting philosophical viewpoints

sentences.text: Pessoa drew the line himself: too radically different from him "to be considered simple pseudonyms", Richard Zenith writes in Literary Hub, his figures were called "heteronyms", and in a "Bibliographical Summary" of 1928, which Zenith and #96 both quote, Pessoa stated that "Pseudonymous works are by the author in his own person, except in the name he signs; heteronymous works are by the author outside his own person", proceeding "from a full-fledged individual created by him, like the lines spoken by a character in a drama he might write"; the version the Poetry Society of America quotes makes the heteronymic work "the work of a complete individuality made up by him".

The field holds the line in the same terms: George Steiner (The Observer, 2001, quoted by Wikipedia) finds pseudonymous writing "not rare in literature or philosophy (Kierkegaard provides a celebrated instance)", while heteronyms "as Pessoa called and defined them, are something different and exceedingly strange", and the Poetry Society account calls it "crucial to make the distinction that Pessoa's "others" were heteronyms rather than pseudonyms".

Wikipedia defines the literary heteronym as "one or more imaginary character(s) created by a writer to write in different styles", differing from pen names, "just false names", in being "characters that have their own supposed physiques, biographies, and writing styles", as Art and Popular Culture also states it; Art and Soul Group calls them "fictitious authors" who "wrote" parts of Pessoa's work; a study in Studi Irlandesi adds world views and the capacity to hold "views in sharp contrast to those of the author who has created them", the heteronymic character presented as "a real man possessing human qualities like all other real men, except one, which is being real itself".

The archive's typology of Pessoa's system (#667) defines the pair as two literary operations: "A pseudonym is a name substitution", "while the writing remains that of the biographical person"; "A heteronym, in Pessoa's sense, is an independent authorial figure with its own biography, poetics, literary lineage, and voice — the writing emerges from a constructed position rather than from the biographical person behind the name"; collapsing them treats Pessoa's practice as "*elaborate pseudonym*", and #666 states heteronymic authorship as the biographical person writing "in a voice not their own, inhabiting an authorial position distinct from themselves".

Other deposits state the line from what the name does: "A pseudonym conceals identity. A heteronym creates it." (#1127); heteronyms are "other names that are also true" (#404); "A pseudonym may hide or rename an author. A heteronym creates a distinct authorial function." (#79); a heteronym "carries a full constructed biography, worldview, and stylistic signature; a pseudonym is a name without that structure" (#761); and #940 defines: "A pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function. A heteronym changes the organization of the authorial function itself.", its markers "testable", a pseudonymic operation failing "one or more", pseudonymy being where "the label changes but the function's organization does not".

The word has other senses: ThoughtCo notes that it "has multiple definitions, depending on its usage referring to grammar, its use in linguistics, or its use in literature", and #921 marks the Habermas–Jauss usage as "technically distinct from the literary practice of *heteronymy* — the production of distinct authorial identities by a single writer, in the lineage of Fernando Pessoa".

#348 and #79 define the heteronym as a function: within the archive's own framework, NH-OS, #348 holds that heteronyms "are not pseudonyms, masks, or personas" but "**authorial functions**", authorship treated "as a system, not a name"; for #79 a heteronym is "a structure-function: a sustained authorial position, internally coherent across style, method, domain, output, and bearing-cost", "validated not by declaration but by performance", "not a false name" but "a true function", and alias capture its opposite, attaching a claimant to an authority-bearing name "without performing the name's function" (#79).

#90 defines it as "a constitutional position — a structurally-defined location from which specific kinds of semantic labor are bearable"; #123, in an analytic sense, as "a stable authorial position that is operationally distinguishable from other authorial positions in the same project", "functionally required by an operation the project is performing" — "The heteronyms are not disguises; they are *operations*"; #794 as "the production of content under a name that is *not the producer's*, with the attributed entity possessing a constructed identity distinct from the producer's own"; and #832 holds that the "I" of a heteronym "is evidence that the heteronymic system includes biographical construction as part of its architecture".

On whether the function is a person the archive's deposits disagree: #96 states "A heteronym is a person.", and limits it, the unconscious heteronym "not a person in the ontological sense this essay defends" for lacking the consciousness "that makes heteronymic practice *practice*"; #90 says of the archive's own heteronyms that they "are not separate persons; they are differentiated positions"; and #136 reports as its parent paper's premise that "a heteronym must survive as a person, with biography, style, chronology, social relation, conflict, and plausible independence; otherwise it is not a heteronym but a transparent pseudonym"; on the mask the sources divide as well: for the Poetry Society account Pessoa's personae "were not so much disguises as extensions and iterations of himself"; #348 holds the heteronyms of NH-OS not masks; #666 that "A single heteronym is a mask; a system of heteronyms is an authorial architecture"; #852 that "The heteronym is a mask: it releases speech into open air".

Beside the heteronyms Wikipedia records two "whom Pessoa called semi-heteronyms, Bernardo Soares and the Baron of Teive", "semi-autobiographical characters who write in prose, "a mere mutilation" of the Pessoa personality", in Pessoa's words to Casais Monteiro (13 January 1935) one whose personality, "although not my own, doesn't differ from my own but is a mere mutilation of it"; the Poetry Society account makes Soares "the closest identity to a pseudonym"; and "There is, lastly, an orthonym, Fernando Pessoa, the namesake of the author, who also considers Caeiro his master", which Art and Soul Group glosses as "the "orthonym," that is, himself", from whom each heteronym is unlike in personality, biography and style.

#667 consolidates these as Pessoa's own categories, the orthonym defined as "The author's own name, but as literary voice — not as biographical person", with the proto-heteronym and para-heteronym by which "Teresa Rita Lopes and subsequent critics have extended the typology", the para-heteronym defined: "A second-order figure operating *within* the heteronymic system, typically as a translator, critic, or commentator on other heteronyms", and a strict heteronym test of five criteria (a distinct proper name; a fictional biography; a distinctive poetics in a substantial body of text; influences other than Pessoa's orthonymic poetics; documented reciprocal relations to other heteronyms); #666 argues that practice under other terminologies "should be recognized as heteronymic when it meets the typological criteria"; #668 finds these categories, "that Pessoa himself articulated", treated as undifferentiated by existing data infrastructure, collapsed into "pseudonym" or flattened "to "heteronym" (as Wikidata currently does)", Wikidata holding as of April 2026 "approximately twenty-five to thirty Pessoa-related items".

The orthonym is defined three further ways and the definitions do not coincide: #123 calls the position bearing "the legal-biological-civil identity of the writer" a definition "contingent on the modern legal-individualist apparatus" and gives "A stronger analytic definition": "the authorial position that bears the project's founding operative gesture, regardless of which substrate or legal identity that position occupies"; #165 makes the distinction one between "*the structural position of singular intent*" and "*the structural position of executory transmission*"; #859 defines the orthonym as "not the real name" but "the regulatory fiction that stabilizes a heteronymic system", Socrates "the central mask through which Plato's authorship is distributed"; on Pessoa's corpus #1561 records the conflict: "Under Pessoa's own usage the orthonym is the position bearing the civil name, which is Pessoa-himself"; under the functional definition it is "arguably Caeiro, the master the other voices acknowledge and organise themselves around"; the seat "records both readings and settles neither".

Pessoa described his enterprise, Poetry International records, as "a drama divided into people instead of into acts" — "the theatre of being" or "drama in people", in Wikipedia — and wrote, the Poetry Society quotes, "I break my soul into pieces," "and into different persons"; the process "began in Pessoa's childhood, gathered steam in his adolescence with the invention of alter egos who wrote in English, and made literary history in 1914" with Caeiro, Campos and Reis, works "over half of which were signed by one of three alter egos, all of whom came into being in 1914", as Zenith puts it; #682 reads the planned "drama em gente" among the acts by which Pessoa "can be read, without irony, as the first modern meta-heteronym", and reads *Orpheu* (1915) as "a meta-heteronymic institution".

Caeiro, Poetry International writes, "the first in the poetic trinity to emerge from Pessoa's soul, was considered the Master of the other two and, indeed, of Pessoa himself"; Wikipedia names him, Reis and Campos the three chief heteronyms, "the latter two consider the former their master", and Art and Soul Group calls Caeiro "the "master" of heteronyms"; #1570 finds that "Every term by which Caeiro is known is ABSENT from Caeiro", paganism, sensationism, objectivism, "*the master*" and sensibility "all supplied by Mora, Campos and Reis"; in Pessoa, #1572 finds, "**The master position is constituted by dying.**"; and #348 states, of heteronyms within NH-OS, that "The death of a heteronym is not failure. It is **formal completion**."

Wikipedia records that the heteronyms "criticise and translate each other's works" and that some "are relatives or know each other"; the Poetry Society account adds that they "collaborated on projects (Crosse worked with his brother, I. I. Crosse)", Poetry International that "There was considerable interaction among the heteronyms", and Steiner finds for each voice an idiom, a biography and "subtle interrelations and reciprocities of awareness"; #1570 reads master–student and heteronymic configuration as "not competing relation-types", a configuration able to "**itself instantiate**" a master–student relation, "**Pessoa is the existence proof**": "A single person can generate genuine asymmetry, inheritance, criticism, development, mastership, discipleship, stylistic separation, and differing conceptual commitments."; they "sometimes intervened in Pessoa's social life": "a jealous Campos wrote letters to the girl" in Pessoa's only attested romance (Art and Popular Culture), and "The largest and most playful of the heteronyms" "even meddled in Pessoa's real-world life" (Poetry International).

The counts run by source and criterion: "at least 70" by "the latest count by Pessoa's editor Teresa Rita Lopes" (Wikipedia); "approximately seventy-two distinct authorial figures" by Lopes's archival work (#667); "about 75 different names" (Studi Irlandesi); "more than seventy personae" (Poetry Society); "over seventy heteronyms" (#1127); "twelve heteronyms, plus one" (#96); and for Zenith "more than one hundred fictitious authors" if the childhood riddlers and humorists are included, "About thirty" signing a significant work, "only three full-fledged heteronyms", the word used "rather loosely", "Authorized by Pessoa's example".

On origin the sources contradict one another: Wikipedia has heteronyms "named and developed" by Pessoa "in the early 20th century" but "thoroughly explored" by Kierkegaard "in the 19th century", who "Had more than a dozen heteronyms with distinct biographies and personalities"; the Studi Irlandesi study credits Pessoa with "the development, naming and introduction of this concept into literature"; #1127 calls him "the Portuguese poet who invented the form"; #96 holds "Fernando Pessoa did not invent heteronymic practice. He formalized it."; and #940, "The practice is not new. What is new is the naming."

#666 reads Pessoa's practice as "not a freak event in literary history but the canonical case of a describable theoretical practice", "Pessoa sits at its apex as the most richly and self-consciously theorized instance, but not as its origin or termination", and holds that Kierkegaard "operated heteronymically in substantively the same sense Pessoa later did, half a century earlier and without the term"; #667 maps Kierkegaard's pseudonymous authors "predominantly to the heteronym category in the extended sense", #940 calls the authorship "more properly heteronymous", and #123 finds Kierkegaard "arguably closer to the Socratic case than Pessoa" — against Steiner, for whom Kierkegaard is the celebrated instance of pseudonymous writing.

On Yeats the Studi Irlandesi study holds, as hypothesis, that "strong heteronymic qualities can also be discerned" in works "some of which produced about twenty years before Pessoa even started his career", finds "three fictional names; Red Hanrahan, Owen Aherne, Michael Robartes", and concludes that "Yeats either originated the concept, albeit without giving it a name, or paved the way", or "could have been a source of inspiration and influence for Pessoa"; Zenith finds "some faint parallels", Yeats's Robartes and Owen Hearne "a duo of "collaborators" with contrasting personalities" and Machado's Juan de Mairena and Abel Martín; #667 places Robartes and Hearne as "occupying a zone between heteronym and literary character", #666 calls them "partial heteronyms", "more developed than pseudonyms, less developed than Pessoa's chief heteronyms", #667 holds Mairena and Martín "heteronymic figures in substantially Pessoan sense" and Borges's Menard "typologically distinct", "a diegetic character with an extradiegetic theoretical function".

The archive draws the lineage further: #1560 seats Browning, Pound and Pessoa as "one practice at three stages of its development", Pound "the middle term, where the mask stops being a character in a poem and becomes a position the poet inhabits"; #263 places the Crimson Hexagon "In the tradition of Browning's and Pound's *Personae*, and approaching Fernando Pessoa's art of the heteronym"; #68's doctrine of the Secret Name names heteronymic practice "a 5,000-year technology for creating new persons through naming", and #96 records its encoding as "a continuous tradition from Pharaonic Titulary (~2600 BCE) through Pessoa to the present day".

Readings of the practice differ: Gaspar Simões, Zenith reports, read it "through a Freudian lens" and "deemed them symptomatic of the author's inability or unwillingness to concentrate his entire self in the act of writing", "a kind of subterfuge, or a gimmick"; the Poetry Society account holds that the conceit "didn't spring from a desire to fool anyone or attract attention", that the selves "were instruments of exorcism and redemption" (Zenith), and that "no one took the ruse as far as Pessoa did—and certainly no one has since"; Zenith holds that "Pessoa staked his very identity on the heteronymous system" and that "no writer can rival" his "glorious if not always harmonious musical ensemble".

#682 states as its central thesis "heteronymy is a technology, not a pathology", holding that Pessoa criticism, "in reading heteronymy primarily through psychology, sensation, or phenomenology, has left open" "the institutional-architectural dimension"; #584 names "the Pessoa reading" as "heteronymy as literary technique, productive, interesting, ultimately aesthetic"; for #1569 heteronymy "on this logic, converts κερματισμός from a wound into a method"; #1658 as "a tool for dividing a mind so that it can make".

#682 defines the meta-heteronym as "a heteronymic system whose personae do not only produce literary works, but the institutional apparatus itself (introductions, criticism, historiography, bibliography) under which those works become legible", its five conditions "necessary together", "A pseudonymous system satisfying C1 but not C2 (Kierkegaard in part) is merely multi-pseudonymous"; it holds that "A hoax is a meta-heteronym that depends on non-disclosure", and limits the reading: "This reading is typological, not causal. It does not claim Pessoa "anticipated" digital infrastructure."; #666 defines the meta-heteronym otherwise, "an inscription that generates heteronyms", and holds, as hypothesis, that heteronyms "may have lives beyond their originating author".

#940 defines heteronymy as "the ethical practice of sustaining a distinct named authorial function without falsely reducing it to a civil identity, and without falsely presenting it as an independent civil person", the authorial function "attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer", and gives the working definition: heteronymy "occurs when a compositional system deliberately constitutes and sustains a named authorial function that is neither identical with nor reducible to the civil bearer, while preserving truthful provenance about the substrates and responsibilities through which that function operates", reading the Caesar/God distinction as "applicable at the authorial layer".

Its limits are #940's own: "Heteronymy is not ethical by its existence. It can also be used to deceive, evade responsibility, fabricate consensus, impersonate independent persons, or multiply one voice into false corroboration"; "False multiplication of the same voice into apparent independent corroboration is not heteronymy in the ethical sense. It is fabrication."; and the deposit's agreement with its own practice "is not, however, verification".

On disclosure #96 holds that "The entire system depends on the practitioner's *consciousness* of the construction"; #1569 finds that both documented heteronymic corpora "announced themselves in print, and those announcements are the **only reason the groupings are known**", so that "A criterion that treats declaration as disqualifying classifies both documented heteronymic corpora as non-heteronymic", and corrects it: "a declaration disqualifies only if it would have been read, at the time, as revealing heteronymic construction".

Outside literature Wikipedia lists David Bowie, who "Systematically employed heteronyms as a performer"; #682 holds that "An Instagram profile is a heteronym"; #96 holds, as hypothesis, that "Facebook turned the *orthonym itself* into a heteronym" "at civilizational scale, without the practitioner's knowledge or consent"; #794 reads an account whose producers "are not concealing their identity (OCEARCH openly manages the account)", attributing content "to an entity that cannot produce content", as "heteronymy in the precise Pessoan sense, extended to the institutional-zoological domain", the non-human attributed case #940 includes "as an experimental edge case rather than as central proof".

#667 introduces "a tentative category — *cross-substrate heteronym*"; #666 states the practice novel, with "no nineteenth- or early-twentieth-century equivalent, because the substrates did not exist", and adds "This is not to claim that Pessoa practiced cross-substrate heteronymy — he did not, and could not."; #667 claims for its typology "adequacy to the practices it was developed to describe", not "cultural universality", and states that classical, certain non-European and oral literatures "may require adjustments the PKG has not yet made".

#123 proposes, as hypothesis, that "the foundational corpus of Western philosophy *can be read as* a single distributed authorial project rather than only as three independent authorships", marks "that this is an analytic category, not a claim about historical self-description", disclaims that "Pessoa-style or CHA-style heteronymy existed as a named or institutionalized practice in classical Athens", offers the archive "as *availability of concept*" and "not as evidence", names "the biological-individuation model of authorship" as the assumption that obscured the configuration, and keeps "the weaker, more defensible" claim: the reading "becomes *thinkable*" and "is not *proven*".

#123 separates pseudepigrapha, which involve "*concealment*: a text is attributed to a figure who did not write it, in order to acquire that figure's authority"; #68 lists an "**Inherited**" named position, "a disciple writes under a teacher's name", the Pauline school among its cases, a "**Split**" one, "one person occupies multiple positions (Pessoa's system; the Dodecad)", and the "**Heteronymic**", "a created name functioning independently"; #203 proposes, as hypothesis, the New Testament authors as "heteronymic author-functions within the Josephan literary system", with its falsifier, the theory "shown to be inapplicable to ancient texts"; and #940 treats Christian transmission as "a heteronymic structure".

#136 states a No-Floor Theorem — under the premise that documentary separateness is constructed by a heteronymic configuration, "the heteronymic method possesses no criterion, internal to itself, for halting the attribution of any adjacent named figure to the configuration" — and reads it: "*it is not a method for discovering identities. It is a method for revealing functional structure.*"; its firewall, "Biographical identity requires evidence. Functional identity requires pattern."; its primary claim, as hypothesis, that institutional scholarship "cannot distinguish ordinary multi-author transmission from mature heteronymic construction using the instruments it currently relies on"; its limit, "*the paper does not assert that the founding corpus was written by one hidden person.*", and "*a configuration may function as a symbolon whether or not it was struck as one*"; #1562, of a two-part Kierkegaard work, finds that "the fit is not stated anywhere inside either half. That is the shape a heteronymic configuration takes".

#1658, later and as hypothesis, names "one self-dividing maker" as the production model the Platonic, Theophrastan and Aristotelian corpus is consistent with, "nothing in it" requiring "another maker" — the maximal form #136 does not assert.

#1560 takes Pessoa, whose letter to Casais Monteiro of 13 January 1935 "attributes the heteronyms, so the grouping is known rather than inferred", as "the positive control for any instrument claiming to detect designed differentiation", and #1562 Kierkegaard as "the second calibration case", who "acknowledged the pseudonymous authorship in print" in 1846 and 1851; #1570 records both as "one-name-one-voice by construction" (Victor Eremita excepted) and Pessoa's minor heteronyms as "unavailable", pt.wikisource carrying "only Caeiro, Reis, Campos and the orthonym".

On these corpora #1570 measures that "Pooling the three heteronyms recovers the orthonym at **0.0258** — inside the M1 same-author band", the best single heteronym Campos at 0.0498 — "Individually the voices do not look like Pessoa; summed, they do.", with a size confound, shaky cross-language comparison and four of about twelve Kierkegaard pseudonymous works seated among its stated limits; and that the reception capture it found on Caeiro "is NOT DISTINCTIVE of heteronymy", occurring "in both classes".
Of the instruments, #1572 finds that "**Relation-type is not recoverable from lexical distribution** — not pupillage, not constructed lineage, not heteronymic construction".

The heteronymic architectures are not one (#1572): "PESSOA CLOSES BY REMAINDER; THE CONFIGURATION WOULD CLOSE BY SUM", a heteronymic series being, as #1571 hypothesizes, "a search downward" in which "Each position subtracts something and tests whether a voice survives the subtraction"; and #1572 limits it: "Two of the best-documented heteronymists built the Socratic structure, and imitation cannot be distinguished from convergence on the cases available."

F1.quote: "The literary concept of the heteronym refers to one or more imaginary character(s) created by a writer to write in different styles."

F2.quote: "Heteronyms differ from pen names (or pseudonyms, from the Greek words for "fake" and "name") in that the latter are just false names, while the former are characters that have their own supposed physiques, biographies, and writing styles."

F3.quote: "Heteronyms were named and developed by the Portuguese writer and poet Fernando Pessoa in the early 20th century, but they were thoroughly explored by the Danish philosopher Kierkegaard in the 19th century and have also been used by other writers."

F4.quote: "In Pessoa's case, there are at least 70 heteronyms (according to the latest count by Pessoa's editor Teresa Rita Lopes)."

F5.quote: "Some of them are relatives or know each other; they criticise and translate each other's works."

F6.quote: "Pessoa's three chief heteronyms are Alberto Caeiro, Ricardo Reis and Álvaro de Campos; the latter two consider the former their master."

F7.quote: "There are also two whom Pessoa called semi-heteronyms, Bernardo Soares and the Baron of Teive, who are semi-autobiographical characters who write in prose, "a mere mutilation" of the Pessoa personality."

F8.quote: "There is, lastly, an orthonym, Fernando Pessoa, the namesake of the author, who also considers Caeiro his master."

F9.quote: "The heteronyms dialogue with each other and even with Pessoa in what he calls "the theatre of being" or "drama in people"."

F10.locus: Fernando Pessoa on the heteronyms (letter to Casais Monteiro, 13.01.1935)
F10.quote: "He's a semi-heteronym because his personality, although not my own, doesn't differ from my own but is a mere mutilation of it."

F11.quote: "Pseudonymous writing is not rare in literature or philosophy (Kierkegaard provides a celebrated instance). 'Heteronyms', as Pessoa called and defined them, are something different and exceedingly strange."

F12.quote: "For each of his 'voices', Pessoa conceived a highly distinctive poetic idiom and technique, a complex biography, a context of literary influence and polemics and, most arrestingly of all, subtle interrelations and reciprocities of awareness."

F13.quote: "Søren Kierkegaard - Had more than a dozen heteronyms with distinct biographies and personalities."

F14.quote: "David Bowie - Systematically employed heteronyms as a performer, his personae changing given the content of the album on which they appear"

F15.quote: "It is crucial to make the distinction that Pessoa's "others" were heteronyms rather than pseudonyms."

F16.quote: "A pseudonymic work is, except for the name with which it is signed, the work of an author writing as himself; a heteronymic work is by an author writing outside his own personality: it is the work of a complete individuality made up by him, just as the utterances of some character in a drama of his would be."

F17.quote: ""I break my soul into pieces," he wrote, "and into different persons.""

F18.quote: "He pretended relentlessly, employing more than seventy personae in his self-searching circus. They were not so much disguises as extensions and iterations of himself."

F19.quote: "His heteronymic conceit didn't spring from a desire to fool anyone or attract attention."

F20.quote: "Yes, Pessoa's heteronyms actually critiqued—sometimes savagely, sometimes kindly—one another's writings. They also collaborated on projects (Crosse worked with his brother, I. I. Crosse) and translated one another's work."

F21.quote: "Then there was the "semi-heteronym" Bernardo Soares, an assistant bookkeeper living in downtown Lisbon who "seems always to be tired or sleepy." He was the closest to Pessoa's own voice, experience, and sensibility, and therefore the closest identity to a pseudonym."

F22.quote: "Pessoa's dozens of constructed alternate selves, Zenith noted, "were instruments of exorcism and redemption."

F23.quote: "Although alter egos had become fashionable accessories for European writers in the early twentieth century, no one took the ruse as far as Pessoa did—and certainly no one has since."

F24.quote: "However, unlike pseudonyms, heteronyms are names given to fully developed characters that, in spite of being imaginary, possess nearly all human qualities such as physical features, biographies, world views, writing styles, etc. – characters that, surprisingly enough, are capable of having views in sharp contrast to those of the author who has created them."

F25.quote: "Fernando Pessoa (1888-1935), arguably one of the most significant literary figures of the 20th century as well as one of the greatest poets in the Portuguese language, is the writer credited with the development, naming and introduction of this concept into literature."

F26.quote: "However, considering the whole body of works produced by the Irish Nobel laureate W.B. Yeats (1865-1939), strong heteronymic qualities can also be discerned in a number of his works some of which produced about twenty years before Pessoa even started his career as a writer."

F27.quote: "In spite of being created by the writer himself, a heteronymic character is presented in such a way that the readers consider him as a completely distinct figure, a real man possessing human qualities like all other real men, except one, which is being real itself."

F28.quote: "Pessoa’s heteronymic system is a rather complex one, with about 75 different names."

F29.quote: "Scanning the collected poems of Yeats, one comes across three fictional names; Red Hanrahan, Owen Aherne, Michael Robartes."

F30.quote: "Even if Pessoa did not borrow from Yeats in creating the concept of heteronym, it is still feasible to think that the heteronymic nature of Yeats’s works could have been a source of inspiration and influence for Pessoa."

F31.quote: "Thus, Yeats either originated the concept, albeit without giving it a name, or paved the way for its introduction into the Western literature that led Pessoa to his important achievement of heteronymic writings"

F32.quote: "The literary concept of heteronym, invented by Portuguese poet Fernando Pessoa, refers to one or more imaginary character(s) created by a poet to write in different styles."

F33.quote: "Heteronyms differ from nom de plumes (or pseudonyms, from the Greek "False Name") in that the latter are just false names, while the former are characters having their own supposed physiques, biographies and writing styles."

F34.quote: "The heteronyms sometimes intervened in Pessoa's social life: during Pessoa's only attested romance, a jealous Campos wrote letters to the girl, who, enjoying the game, wrote back."

F35.quote: "Pessoa left his mark as an extremely original writer for inventing fictitious authors – heteronyms – who “wrote” parts of his work."

F36.quote: "Each one “had” a personality, a biography, a physionomy, a character, a defined literary style, unlike the others and even Pessoa, the “orthonym,” that is, himself."

F37.quote: "Caeiro, the pastoral and (anti)philosophical poet, was the “master” of heteronyms;"

F38.quote: "Too radically different from him to be considered simple pseudonyms, as if only their names had changed, Pessoa called them “heteronyms,”"

F39.quote: "in a “Bibliographical Summary” of his works published in 1928 he explained the conceptual distinction: “Pseudonymous works are by the author in his own person, except in the name he signs; heteronymous works are by the author outside his own person. sentences.text: In literature, one of the term's several senses beside its grammatical and linguistic ones, the concept of the heteronym refers to one or more imaginary characters created by a writer to write in different styles, such as the fictitious authors Fernando Pessoa invented, who "wrote" parts of his work.

Heteronyms differ from pen names, or pseudonyms, in that pseudonyms are just false names while heteronyms are characters with their own supposed physiques, biographies and writing styles; one study adds that they can hold views in sharp contrast to those of the author who created them, and George Steiner, calling pseudonymous writing not rare, with Kierkegaard a celebrated instance, finds "heteronyms", as Pessoa called and defined them, "something different and exceedingly strange".

Pessoa drew the line himself: his figures being too radically different from him to be considered simple pseudonyms, Pessoa called them "heteronyms", Richard Zenith writes, and in a "Bibliographical Summary" published in 1928 Pessoa explained that "Pseudonymous works are by the author in his own person, except in the name he signs; heteronymous works are by the author outside his own person"; a statement the Poetry Society of America quotes has a heteronymic work "by an author writing outside his own personality".

Heteronyms were named and developed by Pessoa in the early twentieth century, the writer credited with introducing the concept into literature, and on Wikipedia's account they were thoroughly explored by Kierkegaard in the nineteenth, who had more than a dozen with distinct biographies and personalities.

Pessoa described his literary enterprise as "a drama divided into people instead of into acts"; the process began in his childhood and made literary history in 1914 with the creation of Alberto Caeiro, Álvaro de Campos and Ricardo Reis, his three chief heteronyms, of whom Caeiro was considered the Master of the other two and of Pessoa himself.

Counts differ: at least 70 heteronyms by the latest count of Pessoa's editor Teresa Rita Lopes, about 75 names in one study, more than seventy personae in another account, and, on Zenith's reckoning, if the childhood riddlers and humorists are included, more than one hundred fictitious authors in whose name Pessoa wrote or at least planned to write, about thirty of whom signed a significant work, with only three full-fledged heteronyms, a word Zenith says he will use "rather loosely", authorized by Pessoa's example.

Beside them Pessoa called Bernardo Soares and the Baron of Teive semi-heteronyms, semi-autobiographical characters who write in prose, "a mere mutilation" of the Pessoa personality, and one account makes Soares the closest identity to a pseudonym; there is, lastly, an orthonym, Fernando Pessoa, the namesake of the author, which one account glosses as Pessoa "himself".

Some of the heteronyms know each other; they criticise and translate each other's works, collaborate on projects and dialogue in what Pessoa calls "drama in people", and in Steiner's description Pessoa conceived for each voice an idiom, a biography and "subtle interrelations and reciprocities of awareness"; they sometimes intervened in Pessoa's social life, a jealous Campos writing letters to the girl in Pessoa's only attested romance.

Readings of the practice differ: Gaspar Simões is reported to have judged the heteronyms a kind of subterfuge, or a gimmick, symptomatic of the author's inability or unwillingness to concentrate his entire self in writing; Zenith holds that Pessoa staked his very identity on the system and that no writer can rival his configured ensemble; the account the Poetry Society excerpts holds that the conceit did not spring from a desire to fool anyone.

Precedents are argued: one study holds that strong heteronymic qualities can be discerned in W. B. Yeats, in works some of which came about twenty years before Pessoa began his career, finds three fictional names in Yeats's collected poems, Red Hanrahan, Owen Aherne and Michael Robartes, and concludes that Yeats either originated the concept without naming it or paved the way for its introduction into Western literature, finding it feasible to think that Yeats's works could have been a source of inspiration even if Pessoa did not borrow from him; Zenith finds "some faint parallels", Yeats's Robartes and Owen Hearne and Antonio Machado's Juan de Mairena and Abel Martín.

L_BA.text: Pessoa drew the line himself: too radically different from him "to be considered simple pseudonyms", Richard Zenith writes in Literary Hub, his figures were called "heteronyms", and in a "Bibliographical Summary" of 1928, which Zenith and #96 both quote, Pessoa stated that "Pseudonymous works are by the author in his own person, except in the name he signs; heteronymous works are by the author outside his own person", proceeding "from a full-fledged individual created by him, like the lines spoken by a character in a drama he might write"; the version the Poetry Society of America quotes makes the heteronymic work "the work of a complete individuality made up by him". The field holds the line in the same terms: George Steiner (The Observer, 2001, quoted by Wikipedia) finds pseudonymous writing "not rare in literature or philosophy (Kierkegaard provides a celebrated instance)", while heteronyms "as Pessoa called and defined them, are something different and exceedingly strange", and the Poetry Society account calls it "crucial to make the distinction that Pessoa's "others" were heteronyms rather than pseudonyms". Wikipedia defines the literary heteronym as "one or more imaginary character(s) created by a writer to write in different styles", differing from pen names, "just false names", in being "characters that have their own supposed physiques, biographies, and writing styles", as Art and Popular Culture also states it; Art and Soul Group calls them "fictitious authors" who "wrote" parts of Pessoa's work; a study in Studi Irlandesi adds world views and the capacity to hold "views in sharp contrast to those of the author who has created them", the heteronymic character presented as "a real man possessing human qualities like all other real men, except one, which is being real itself". The archive's typology of Pessoa's system (#667) defines the pair as two literary operations: "A pseudonym is a name substitution", "while the writing remains that of the biographical person"; "A heteronym, in Pessoa's sense, is an independent authorial figure with its own biography, poetics, literary lineage, and voice — the writing emerges from a constructed position rather than from the biographical person behind the name"; collapsing them treats Pessoa's practice as "*elaborate pseudonym*", and #666 states heteronymic authorship as the biographical person writing "in a voice not their own, inhabiting an authorial position distinct from themselves". Other deposits state the line from what the name does: "A pseudonym conceals identity. A heteronym creates it." (#1127); heteronyms are "other names that are also true" (#404); "A pseudonym may hide or rename an author. A heteronym creates a distinct authorial function." (#79); a heteronym "carries a full constructed biography, worldview, and stylistic signature; a pseudonym is a name without that structure" (#761); and #940 defines: "A pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function. A heteronym changes the organization of the authorial function itself.", its markers "testable", a pseudonymic operation failing "one or more", pseudonymy being where "the label changes but the function's organization does not". The word has other senses: ThoughtCo notes that it "has multiple definitions, depending on its usage referring to grammar, its use in linguistics, or its use in literature", and #921 marks the Habermas–Jauss usage as "technically distinct from the literary practice of *heteronymy* — the production of distinct authorial identities by a single writer, in the lineage of Fernando Pessoa". #348 and #79 define the heteronym as a function: within the archive's own framework, NH-OS, #348 holds that heteronyms "are not pseudonyms, masks, or personas" but "**authorial functions**", authorship treated "as a system, not a name"; for #79 a heteronym is "a structure-function: a sustained authorial position, internally coherent across style, method, domain, output, and bearing-cost", "validated not by declaration but by performance", "not a false name" but "a true function", and alias capture its opposite, attaching a claimant to an authority-bearing name "without performing the name's function" (#79). #90 defines it as "a constitutional position — a structurally-defined location from which specific kinds of semantic labor are bearable"; #123, in an analytic sense, as "a stable authorial position that is operationally distinguishable from other authorial positions in the same project", "functionally required by an operation the project is performing" — "The heteronyms are not disguises; they are *operations*"; #794 as "the production of content under a name that is *not the producer's*, with the attributed entity possessing a constructed identity distinct from the producer's own"; and #832 holds that the "I" of a heteronym "is evidence that the heteronymic system includes biographical construction as part of its architecture". On whether the function is a person the archive's deposits disagree: #96 states "A heteronym is a person.", and limits it, the unconscious heteronym "not a person in the ontological sense this essay defends" for lacking the consciousness "that makes heteronymic practice *practice*"; #90 says of the archive's own heteronyms that they "are not separate persons; they are differentiated positions"; and #136 reports as its parent paper's premise that "a heteronym must survive as a person, with biography, style, chronology, social relation, conflict, and plausible independence; otherwise it is not a heteronym but a transparent pseudonym"; on the mask the sources divide as well: for the Poetry Society account Pessoa's personae "were not so much disguises as extensions and iterations of himself"; #348 holds the heteronyms of NH-OS not masks; #666 that "A single heteronym is a mask; a system of heteronyms is an authorial architecture"; #852 that "The heteronym is a mask: it releases speech into open air". Beside the heteronyms Wikipedia records two "whom Pessoa called semi-heteronyms, Bernardo Soares and the Baron of Teive", "semi-autobiographical characters who write in prose, "a mere mutilation" of the Pessoa personality", in Pessoa's words to Casais Monteiro (13 January 1935) one whose personality, "although not my own, doesn't differ from my own but is a mere mutilation of it"; the Poetry Society account makes Soares "the closest identity to a pseudonym"; and "There is, lastly, an orthonym, Fernando Pessoa, the namesake of the author, who also considers Caeiro his master", which Art and Soul Group glosses as "the "orthonym," that is, himself", from whom each heteronym is unlike in personality, biography and style. #667 consolidates these as Pessoa's own categories, the orthonym defined as "The author's own name, but as literary voice — not as biographical person", with the proto-heteronym and para-heteronym by which "Teresa Rita Lopes and subsequent critics have extended the typology", the para-heteronym defined: "A second-order figure operating *within* the heteronymic system, typically as a translator, critic, or commentator on other heteronyms", and a strict heteronym test of five criteria (a distinct proper name; a fictional biography; a distinctive poetics in a substantial body of text; influences other than Pessoa's orthonymic poetics; documented reciprocal relations to other heteronyms); #666 argues that practice under other terminologies "should be recognized as heteronymic when it meets the typological criteria"; #668 finds these categories, "that Pessoa himself articulated", treated as undifferentiated by existing data infrastructure, collapsed into "pseudonym" or flattened "to "heteronym" (as Wikidata currently does)", Wikidata holding as of April 2026 "approximately twenty-five to thirty Pessoa-related items". The orthonym is defined three further ways and the definitions do not coincide: #123 calls the position bearing "the legal-biological-civil identity of the writer" a definition "contingent on the modern legal-individualist apparatus" and gives "A stronger analytic definition": "the authorial position that bears the project's founding operative gesture, regardless of which substrate or legal identity that position occupies"; #165 makes the distinction one between "*the structural position of singular intent*" and "*the structural position of executory transmission*"; #859 defines the orthonym as "not the real name" but "the regulatory fiction that stabilizes a heteronymic system", Socrates "the central mask through which Plato's authorship is distributed"; on Pessoa's corpus #1561 records the conflict: "Under Pessoa's own usage the orthonym is the position bearing the civil name, which is Pessoa-himself"; under the functional definition it is "arguably Caeiro, the master the other voices acknowledge and organise themselves around"; the seat "records both readings and settles neither". Pessoa described his enterprise, Poetry International records, as "a drama divided into people instead of into acts" — "the theatre of being" or "drama in people", in Wikipedia — and wrote, the Poetry Society quotes, "I break my soul into pieces," "and into different persons"; the process "began in Pessoa's childhood, gathered steam in his adolescence with the invention of alter egos who wrote in English, and made literary history in 1914" with Caeiro, Campos and Reis, works "over half of which were signed by one of three alter egos, all of whom came into being in 1914", as Zenith puts it; #682 reads the planned "drama em gente" among the acts by which Pessoa "can be read, without irony, as the first modern meta-heteronym", and reads *Orpheu* (1915) as "a meta-heteronymic institution". Caeiro, Poetry International writes, "the first in the poetic trinity to emerge from Pessoa's soul, was considered the Master of the other two and, indeed, of Pessoa himself"; Wikipedia names him, Reis and Campos the three chief heteronyms, "the latter two consider the former their master", and Art and Soul Group calls Caeiro "the "master" of heteronyms"; #1570 finds that "Every term by which Caeiro is known is ABSENT from Caeiro", paganism, sensationism, objectivism, "*the master*" and sensibility "all supplied by Mora, Campos and Reis"; in Pessoa, #1572 finds, "**The master position is constituted by dying.**"; and #348 states, of heteronyms within NH-OS, that "The death of a heteronym is not failure. It is **formal completion**." Wikipedia records that the heteronyms "criticise and translate each other's works" and that some "are relatives or know each other"; the Poetry Society account adds that they "collaborated on projects (Crosse worked with his brother, I. I. Crosse)", Poetry International that "There was considerable interaction among the heteronyms", and Steiner finds for each voice an idiom, a biography and "subtle interrelations and reciprocities of awareness"; #1570 reads master–student and heteronymic configuration as "not competing relation-types", a configuration able to "**itself instantiate**" a master–student relation, "**Pessoa is the existence proof**": "A single person can generate genuine asymmetry, inheritance, criticism, development, mastership, discipleship, stylistic separation, and differing conceptual commitments."; they "sometimes intervened in Pessoa's social life": "a jealous Campos wrote letters to the girl" in Pessoa's only attested romance (Art and Popular Culture), and "The largest and most playful of the heteronyms" "even meddled in Pessoa's real-world life" (Poetry International). The counts run by source and criterion: "at least 70" by "the latest count by Pessoa's editor Teresa Rita Lopes" (Wikipedia); "approximately seventy-two distinct authorial figures" by Lopes's archival work (#667); "about 75 different names" (Studi Irlandesi); "more than seventy personae" (Poetry Society); "over seventy heteronyms" (#1127); "twelve heteronyms, plus one" (#96); and for Zenith "more than one hundred fictitious authors" if the childhood riddlers and humorists are included, "About thirty" signing a significant work, "only three full-fledged heteronyms", the word used "rather loosely", "Authorized by Pessoa's example". On origin the sources contradict one another: Wikipedia has heteronyms "named and developed" by Pessoa "in the early 20th century" but "thoroughly explored" by Kierkegaard "in the 19th century", who "Had more than a dozen heteronyms with distinct biographies and personalities"; the Studi Irlandesi study credits Pessoa with "the development, naming and introduction of this concept into literature"; #1127 calls him "the Portuguese poet who invented the form"; #96 holds "Fernando Pessoa did not invent heteronymic practice. He formalized it."; and #940, "The practice is not new. What is new is the naming." #666 reads Pessoa's practice as "not a freak event in literary history but the canonical case of a describable theoretical practice", "Pessoa sits at its apex as the most richly and self-consciously theorized instance, but not as its origin or termination", and holds that Kierkegaard "operated heteronymically in substantively the same sense Pessoa later did, half a century earlier and without the term"; #667 maps Kierkegaard's pseudonymous authors "predominantly to the heteronym category in the extended sense", #940 calls the authorship "more properly heteronymous", and #123 finds Kierkegaard "arguably closer to the Socratic case than Pessoa" — against Steiner, for whom Kierkegaard is the celebrated instance of pseudonymous writing. On Yeats the Studi Irlandesi study holds, as hypothesis, that "strong heteronymic qualities can also be discerned" in works "some of which produced about twenty years before Pessoa even started his career", finds "three fictional names; Red Hanrahan, Owen Aherne, Michael Robartes", and concludes that "Yeats either originated the concept, albeit without giving it a name, or paved the way", or "could have been a source of inspiration and influence for Pessoa"; Zenith finds "some faint parallels", Yeats's Robartes and Owen Hearne "a duo of "collaborators" with contrasting personalities" and Machado's Juan de Mairena and Abel Martín; #667 places Robartes and Hearne as "occupying a zone between heteronym and literary character", #666 calls them "partial heteronyms", "more developed than pseudonyms, less developed than Pessoa's chief heteronyms", #667 holds Mairena and Martín "heteronymic figures in substantially Pessoan sense" and Borges's Menard "typologically distinct", "a diegetic character with an extradiegetic theoretical function". The archive draws the lineage further: #1560 seats Browning, Pound and Pessoa as "one practice at three stages of its development", Pound "the middle term, where the mask stops being a character in a poem and becomes a position the poet inhabits"; #263 places the Crimson Hexagon "In the tradition of Browning's and Pound's *Personae*, and approaching Fernando Pessoa's art of the heteronym"; #68's doctrine of the Secret Name names heteronymic practice "a 5,000-year technology for creating new persons through naming", and #96 records its encoding as "a continuous tradition from Pharaonic Titulary (~2600 BCE) through Pessoa to the present day". Readings of the practice differ: Gaspar Simões, Zenith reports, read it "through a Freudian lens" and "deemed them symptomatic of the author's inability or unwillingness to concentrate his entire self in the act of writing", "a kind of subterfuge, or a gimmick"; the Poetry Society account holds that the conceit "didn't spring from a desire to fool anyone or attract attention", that the selves "were instruments of exorcism and redemption" (Zenith), and that "no one took the ruse as far as Pessoa did—and certainly no one has since"; Zenith holds that "Pessoa staked his very identity on the heteronymous system" and that "no writer can rival" his "glorious if not always harmonious musical ensemble". #682 states as its central thesis "heteronymy is a technology, not a pathology", holding that Pessoa criticism, "in reading heteronymy primarily through psychology, sensation, or phenomenology, has left open" "the institutional-architectural dimension"; #584 names "the Pessoa reading" as "heteronymy as literary technique, productive, interesting, ultimately aesthetic"; for #1569 heteronymy "on this logic, converts κερματισμός from a wound into a method"; #1658 as "a tool for dividing a mind so that it can make". #682 defines the meta-heteronym as "a heteronymic system whose personae do not only produce literary works, but the institutional apparatus itself (introductions, criticism, historiography, bibliography) under which those works become legible", its five conditions "necessary together", "A pseudonymous system satisfying C1 but not C2 (Kierkegaard in part) is merely multi-pseudonymous"; it holds that "A hoax is a meta-heteronym that depends on non-disclosure", and limits the reading: "This reading is typological, not causal. It does not claim Pessoa "anticipated" digital infrastructure."; #666 defines the meta-heteronym otherwise, "an inscription that generates heteronyms", and holds, as hypothesis, that heteronyms "may have lives beyond their originating author". #940 defines heteronymy as "the ethical practice of sustaining a distinct named authorial function without falsely reducing it to a civil identity, and without falsely presenting it as an independent civil person", the authorial function "attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer", and gives the working definition: heteronymy "occurs when a compositional system deliberately constitutes and sustains a named authorial function that is neither identical with nor reducible to the civil bearer, while preserving truthful provenance about the substrates and responsibilities through which that function operates", reading the Caesar/God distinction as "applicable at the authorial layer". Its limits are #940's own: "Heteronymy is not ethical by its existence. It can also be used to deceive, evade responsibility, fabricate consensus, impersonate independent persons, or multiply one voice into false corroboration"; "False multiplication of the same voice into apparent independent corroboration is not heteronymy in the ethical sense. It is fabrication."; and the deposit's agreement with its own practice "is not, however, verification". On disclosure #96 holds that "The entire system depends on the practitioner's *consciousness* of the construction"; #1569 finds that both documented heteronymic corpora "announced themselves in print, and those announcements are the **only reason the groupings are known**", so that "A criterion that treats declaration as disqualifying classifies both documented heteronymic corpora as non-heteronymic", and corrects it: "a declaration disqualifies only if it would have been read, at the time, as revealing heteronymic construction". Outside literature Wikipedia lists David Bowie, who "Systematically employed heteronyms as a performer"; #682 holds that "An Instagram profile is a heteronym"; #96 holds, as hypothesis, that "Facebook turned the *orthonym itself* into a heteronym" "at civilizational scale, without the practitioner's knowledge or consent"; #794 reads an account whose producers "are not concealing their identity (OCEARCH openly manages the account)", attributing content "to an entity that cannot produce content", as "heteronymy in the precise Pessoan sense, extended to the institutional-zoological domain", the non-human attributed case #940 includes "as an experimental edge case rather than as central proof". #667 introduces "a tentative category — *cross-substrate heteronym*"; #666 states the practice novel, with "no nineteenth- or early-twentieth-century equivalent, because the substrates did not exist", and adds "This is not to claim that Pessoa practiced cross-substrate heteronymy — he did not, and could not."; #667 claims for its typology "adequacy to the practices it was developed to describe", not "cultural universality", and states that classical, certain non-European and oral literatures "may require adjustments the PKG has not yet made". #123 proposes, as hypothesis, that "the foundational corpus of Western philosophy *can be read as* a single distributed authorial project rather than only as three independent authorships", marks "that this is an analytic category, not a claim about historical self-description", disclaims that "Pessoa-style or CHA-style heteronymy existed as a named or institutionalized practice in classical Athens", offers the archive "as *availability of concept*" and "not as evidence", names "the biological-individuation model of authorship" as the assumption that obscured the configuration, and keeps "the weaker, more defensible" claim: the reading "becomes *thinkable*" and "is not *proven*". #123 separates pseudepigrapha, which involve "*concealment*: a text is attributed to a figure who did not write it, in order to acquire that figure's authority"; #68 lists an "**Inherited**" named position, "a disciple writes under a teacher's name", the Pauline school among its cases, a "**Split**" one, "one person occupies multiple positions (Pessoa's system; the Dodecad)", and the "**Heteronymic**", "a created name functioning independently"; #203 proposes, as hypothesis, the New Testament authors as "heteronymic author-functions within the Josephan literary system", with its falsifier, the theory "shown to be inapplicable to ancient texts"; and #940 treats Christian transmission as "a heteronymic structure". #136 states a No-Floor Theorem — under the premise that documentary separateness is constructed by a heteronymic configuration, "the heteronymic method possesses no criterion, internal to itself, for halting the attribution of any adjacent named figure to the configuration" — and reads it: "*it is not a method for discovering identities. It is a method for revealing functional structure.*"; its firewall, "Biographical identity requires evidence. Functional identity requires pattern."; its primary claim, as hypothesis, that institutional scholarship "cannot distinguish ordinary multi-author transmission from mature heteronymic construction using the instruments it currently relies on"; its limit, "*the paper does not assert that the founding corpus was written by one hidden person.*", and "*a configuration may function as a symbolon whether or not it was struck as one*"; #1562, of a two-part Kierkegaard work, finds that "the fit is not stated anywhere inside either half. That is the shape a heteronymic configuration takes". #1658, later and as hypothesis, names "one self-dividing maker" as the production model the Platonic, Theophrastan and Aristotelian corpus is consistent with, "nothing in it" requiring "another maker" — the maximal form #136 does not assert. #1560 takes Pessoa, whose letter to Casais Monteiro of 13 January 1935 "attributes the heteronyms, so the grouping is known rather than inferred", as "the positive control for any instrument claiming to detect designed differentiation", and #1562 Kierkegaard as "the second calibration case", who "acknowledged the pseudonymous authorship in print" in 1846 and 1851; #1570 records both as "one-name-one-voice by construction" (Victor Eremita excepted) and Pessoa's minor heteronyms as "unavailable", pt.wikisource carrying "only Caeiro, Reis, Campos and the orthonym". On these corpora #1570 measures that "Pooling the three heteronyms recovers the orthonym at **0.0258** — inside the M1 same-author band", the best single heteronym Campos at 0.0498 — "Individually the voices do not look like Pessoa; summed, they do.", with a size confound, shaky cross-language comparison and four of about twelve Kierkegaard pseudonymous works seated among its stated limits; and that the reception capture it found on Caeiro "is NOT DISTINCTIVE of heteronymy", occurring "in both classes". Of the instruments, #1572 finds that "**Relation-type is not recoverable from lexical distribution** — not pupillage, not constructed lineage, not heteronymic construction". The heteronymic architectures are not one (#1572): "PESSOA CLOSES BY REMAINDER; THE CONFIGURATION WOULD CLOSE BY SUM", a heteronymic series being, as #1571 hypothesizes, "a search downward" in which "Each position subtracts something and tests whether a voice survives the subtraction"; and #1572 limits it: "Two of the best-documented heteronymists built the Socratic structure, and imitation cannot be distinguished from convergence on the cases available."

F1.quote: "The literary concept of the heteronym refers to one or more imaginary character(s) created by a writer to write in different styles."

F2.quote: "Heteronyms differ from pen names (or pseudonyms, from the Greek words for "fake" and "name") in that the latter are just false names, while the former are characters that have their own supposed physiques, biographies, and writing styles."

F3.quote: "Heteronyms were named and developed by the Portuguese writer and poet Fernando Pessoa in the early 20th century, but they were thoroughly explored by the Danish philosopher Kierkegaard in the 19th century and have also been used by other writers."

F4.quote: "In Pessoa's case, there are at least 70 heteronyms (according to the latest count by Pessoa's editor Teresa Rita Lopes)."

F5.quote: "Some of them are relatives or know each other; they criticise and translate each other's works."

F6.quote: "Pessoa's three chief heteronyms are Alberto Caeiro, Ricardo Reis and Álvaro de Campos; the latter two consider the former their master."

F7.quote: "There are also two whom Pessoa called semi-heteronyms, Bernardo Soares and the Baron of Teive, who are semi-autobiographical characters who write in prose, "a mere mutilation" of the Pessoa personality."

F8.quote: "There is, lastly, an orthonym, Fernando Pessoa, the namesake of the author, who also considers Caeiro his master."

F9.quote: "The heteronyms dialogue with each other and even with Pessoa in what he calls "the theatre of being" or "drama in people"."

F10.locus: Fernando Pessoa on the heteronyms (letter to Casais Monteiro, 13.01.1935)
F10.quote: "He's a semi-heteronym because his personality, although not my own, doesn't differ from my own but is a mere mutilation of it."

F11.quote: "Pseudonymous writing is not rare in literature or philosophy (Kierkegaard provides a celebrated instance). 'Heteronyms', as Pessoa called and defined them, are something different and exceedingly strange."

F12.quote: "For each of his 'voices', Pessoa conceived a highly distinctive poetic idiom and technique, a complex biography, a context of literary influence and polemics and, most arrestingly of all, subtle interrelations and reciprocities of awareness."

F13.quote: "Søren Kierkegaard - Had more than a dozen heteronyms with distinct biographies and personalities."

F14.quote: "David Bowie - Systematically employed heteronyms as a performer, his personae changing given the content of the album on which they appear"

F15.quote: "It is crucial to make the distinction that Pessoa's "others" were heteronyms rather than pseudonyms."

F16.quote: "A pseudonymic work is, except for the name with which it is signed, the work of an author writing as himself; a heteronymic work is by an author writing outside his own personality: it is the work of a complete individuality made up by him, just as the utterances of some character in a drama of his would be."

F17.quote: ""I break my soul into pieces," he wrote, "and into different persons.""

F18.quote: "He pretended relentlessly, employing more than seventy personae in his self-searching circus. They were not so much disguises as extensions and iterations of himself."

F19.quote: "His heteronymic conceit didn't spring from a desire to fool anyone or attract attention."

F20.quote: "Yes, Pessoa's heteronyms actually critiqued—sometimes savagely, sometimes kindly—one another's writings. They also collaborated on projects (Crosse worked with his brother, I. I. Crosse) and translated one another's work."

F21.quote: "Then there was the "semi-heteronym" Bernardo Soares, an assistant bookkeeper living in downtown Lisbon who "seems always to be tired or sleepy." He was the closest to Pessoa's own voice, experience, and sensibility, and therefore the closest identity to a pseudonym."

sentences.text: In literature, one of the term's several senses beside its grammatical and linguistic ones, the concept of the heteronym refers to one or more imaginary characters created by a writer to write in different styles, such as the fictitious authors Fernando Pessoa invented, who "wrote" parts of his work.

Heteronyms differ from pen names, or pseudonyms, in that pseudonyms are just false names while heteronyms are characters with their own supposed physiques, biographies and writing styles; one study adds that they can hold views in sharp contrast to those of the author who created them, and George Steiner, calling pseudonymous writing not rare, with Kierkegaard a celebrated instance, finds "heteronyms", as Pessoa called and defined them, "something different and exceedingly strange".

Pessoa drew the line himself: his figures being too radically different from him to be considered simple pseudonyms, Pessoa called them "heteronyms", Richard Zenith writes, and in a "Bibliographical Summary" published in 1928 Pessoa explained that "Pseudonymous works are by the author in his own person, except in the name he signs; heteronymous works are by the author outside his own person"; a statement the Poetry Society of America quotes has a heteronymic work "by an author writing outside his own personality".

Heteronyms were named and developed by Pessoa in the early twentieth century, the writer credited with introducing the concept into literature, and on Wikipedia's account they were thoroughly explored by Kierkegaard in the nineteenth, who had more than a dozen with distinct biographies and personalities.

Pessoa described his literary enterprise as "a drama divided into people instead of into acts"; the process began in his childhood and made literary history in 1914 with the creation of Alberto Caeiro, Álvaro de Campos and Ricardo Reis, his three chief heteronyms, of whom Caeiro was considered the Master of the other two and of Pessoa himself.

Counts differ: at least 70 heteronyms by the latest count of Pessoa's editor Teresa Rita Lopes, about 75 names in one study, more than seventy personae in another account, and, on Zenith's reckoning, if the childhood riddlers and humorists are included, more than one hundred fictitious authors in whose name Pessoa wrote or at least planned to write, about thirty of whom signed a significant work, with only three full-fledged heteronyms, a word Zenith says he will use "rather loosely", authorized by Pessoa's example.

Beside them Pessoa called Bernardo Soares and the Baron of Teive semi-heteronyms, semi-autobiographical characters who write in prose, "a mere mutilation" of the Pessoa personality, and one account makes Soares the closest identity to a pseudonym; there is, lastly, an orthonym, Fernando Pessoa, the namesake of the author, which one account glosses as Pessoa "himself".

Some of the heteronyms know each other; they criticise and translate each other's works, collaborate on projects and dialogue in what Pessoa calls "drama in people", and in Steiner's description Pessoa conceived for each voice an idiom, a biography and "subtle interrelations and reciprocities of awareness"; they sometimes intervened in Pessoa's social life, a jealous Campos writing letters to the girl in Pessoa's only attested romance.

Readings of the practice differ: Gaspar Simões is reported to have judged the heteronyms a kind of subterfuge, or a gimmick, symptomatic of the author's inability or unwillingness to concentrate his entire self in writing; Zenith holds that Pessoa staked his very identity on the system and that no writer can rival his configured ensemble; the account the Poetry Society excerpts holds that the conceit did not spring from a desire to fool anyone.

Precedents are argued: one study holds that strong heteronymic qualities can be discerned in W. B. Yeats, in works some of which came about twenty years before Pessoa began his career, finds three fictional names in Yeats's collected poems, Red Hanrahan, Owen Aherne and Michael Robartes, and concludes that Yeats either originated the concept without naming it or paved the way for its introduction into Western literature, finding it feasible to think that Yeats's works could have been a source of inspiration even if Pessoa did not borrow from him; Zenith finds "some faint parallels", Yeats's Robartes and Owen Hearne and Antonio Machado's Juan de Mairena and Abel Martín.

A further position, the archive's typology of Pessoa's system, states the distinction as definition: a pseudonym is defined as a name substitution in which the writing remains that of the biographical person, a heteronym in Pessoa's sense as an independent authorial figure whose writing emerges from a constructed position, and the orthonym as the author's own name as literary voice, apart from the biographical person; Teresa Rita Lopes and later critics are reported to have extended the typology with the proto-heteronym and the para-heteronym, and a strict heteronym test of five criteria is specified.

The typology claims adequacy to the practices it was developed to describe, disclaims cultural universality, and states that classical literatures, certain non-European traditions and oral traditions may require adjustments it has not yet made; within it Kierkegaard's pseudonymous authors are read as mapping predominantly to the heteronym in the extended sense, Machado's Mairena and Martín are held heteronymic in substantially Pessoan sense, Borges's Menard is held typologically distinct, a diegetic character, and Yeats's Robartes and Hearne are placed in a zone between heteronym and literary character.

Another archive paper holds Pessoa's practice the canonical case of a describable theoretical practice, a practice with a history, Pessoa its most richly theorized instance though neither its origin nor its termination, and Kierkegaard as having operated heteronymically in substantively Pessoa's sense half a century earlier and without the term; on origins the archive is divided, one deposit calling Pessoa the poet "who invented the form" and another holding that he "did not invent heteronymic practice. He formalized it."

One essay defines the meta-heteronym as a heteronymic system whose personae produce, beyond literary works, the institutional apparatus under which those works become legible, reads Orpheu (1915) as such an institution, holds that Pessoa can be read as the first modern meta-heteronym, and states as its central thesis "heteronymy is a technology, not a pathology", describing its reading as typological and disclaiming that Pessoa "anticipated" digital infrastructure; another deposit holds the meta-heteronym to be "an inscription that generates heteronyms".

Several archive deposits define the heteronym as a function: heteronyms as "authorial functions", a heteronym as "a structure-function" validated by performance, and, in a further pair of definitions, a pseudonym as changing the label attached to an authorial function and a heteronym as changing its organization.

The archive is divided on what the heteronym is: one essay states that "A heteronym is a person", while a registry says of the archive's own heteronyms that they "are not separate persons; they are differentiated positions" through which their bearer's labour is articulated, and a further paper reports as its parent paper's central premise that a heteronym must "survive as a person", with biography, style and plausible independence, or be a transparent pseudonym; on the mask, one deposit holds heteronyms to be "not pseudonyms, masks, or personas", while another holds that "A single heteronym is a mask; a system of heteronyms is an authorial architecture" and a third that "The heteronym is a mask".

An ethics paper defines heteronymy as the ethical practice of sustaining a distinct named authorial function without falsely reducing it to a civil identity or falsely presenting it as an independent civil person, holds the function attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer, and states its limits: heteronymy "is not ethical by its existence", and the false multiplication of one voice into apparent independent corroboration is stated to be fabrication.

The orthonym is contested within the archive: it is defined as the author's own name as literary voice, as the authorial position bearing a project's founding operative gesture, which on Pessoa's corpus is "arguably Caeiro" under the functional definition and Pessoa-himself under Pessoa's usage, a corpus seat recording both readings and settling neither, and as "the regulatory fiction that stabilizes a heteronymic system", with Socrates as the central mask through which Plato's authorship is distributed.

A paper on the Socratic corpus states as hypothesis that the founding corpus of Western philosophy can be read as a single distributed authorial project, defines the heteronym analytically as a stable authorial position functionally required by an operation the project performs, distinguishes pseudepigrapha by concealment, and limits its claim to the reading becoming thinkable, disclaiming that Pessoa-style heteronymy existed as a named or institutionalized practice in classical Athens; a further deposit, without reference to concealment, lists an "Inherited" named position, in which a disciple writes under a teacher's name, the Pauline school among its cases, separately from the "Heteronymic" position, a created name functioning independently.

A further paper states a No-Floor Theorem, that under the premise that documentary separateness is constructed by a heteronymic configuration the method has no internal criterion for halting attribution of adjacent named figures, sets a firewall, "Biographical identity requires evidence. Functional identity requires pattern.", and does not assert that the founding corpus was written by one hidden person; on maker-count the archive is divided, another paper proposing as hypothesis "one self-dividing maker" as the production model with which the Platonic, Theophrastan and Aristotelian corpus is consistent, "nothing in it" requiring another maker.

The archive seats Browning, Pound and Pessoa as "one practice at three stages", Pound read as the middle term where the mask becomes a position the poet inhabits, and takes Pessoa, whose letter of 13 January 1935 attributes the heteronyms, as the positive control for instruments claiming to detect designed differentiation, Kierkegaard's printed acknowledgements of 1846 and 1851 making his grouping documented in the same way.

On these corpora a measure finds that pooling Pessoa's three heteronyms recovers the orthonym inside the same-author band while individually the voices do not look like Pessoa, a size confound among its stated limits; that every term by which Caeiro is known is absent from Caeiro's own text, supplied by Mora, Campos and Reis, a capture the register then records as not distinctive of heteronymy; and that relation-type, heteronymic construction included, is not recoverable from lexical distribution; from these results the register reads a heteronymic configuration as able to instantiate a master–student relation, Pessoa being "the existence proof".
